COVID-19 Case and Death Analysis in the United States Using Johns Hopkins (JHU) Center for Systems Science and Engineering (CSSE) Data

MSDS Student

2026-10-08

Analysis of the COVID-19 Case and Death Dataset

This report analyzes US COVID-19 data from the Johns Hopkins University (JHU) Center for Systems Science and Engineering (CSSE) COVID-19 Data Repository on GitHub. The repository contains daily cumulative confirmed cases and deaths globally and for US counties. Two time series files are used: US confirmed cases and US deaths. JHU stopped updating this data in March 2023 and the dataset runs from January 22, 2020 through March 9, 2023.

Questions of Interest:

  • How did COVID-19 cases and deaths change over time in the US as a whole and in specific states?
  • How do states compare in deaths per thousand residents?
  • Does a state’s death rate relate to a state’s case rate?

Data sources:

  • Source: JHU CSSE COVID-19 Data
  • Time series data folder: csse_covid_19_time_series

Guide to using the comments in this report: The first line of each code chunk is a comment saying where the code comes from. Much of the material in this report comes from lectures from CU Boulder’s DTSA 5301 Data Science as a Field course. If code is directly from the lecture, a comment before that chunk of code says: # from class lectures. Some of these codes might be slightly modified from class due to changes in the dataset since the lectures occurred. New analysis that was done beyond the class lectures is labeled # new analysis.

Importing the data

First, we’ll load the required packages.

# from class lectures
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)

Next, we’ll build the web addresses for the two data files.

# from class lectures with updated URL 
url_in <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CSSEGISandData/COVID-19/refs/heads/master/csse_covid_19_data/csse_covid_19_time_series/"
file_names <- c("time_series_covid19_confirmed_US.csv",
                "time_series_covid19_deaths_US.csv")
urls <- str_c(url_in, file_names)

Next, we’ll read in the two files.

# from class lectures but only the US is read in for this analysis
US_cases <- read_csv(urls[1])
US_deaths <- read_csv(urls[2])

Tidying and Transforming the Data

We’ll check which columns US_deaths has that US_cases does not:

# new analysis
setdiff(names(US_deaths), names(US_cases))
## [1] "Population"

The only difference is Population.

Next, each date gets its own row with date and cases (or deaths) as columns. We’ll pivot the date columns. We will also narrow the range to Admin2 through cases, convert date from text to date format, and drop Lat and Long_.

# from class lectures
US_cases <- US_cases %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -(UID:Combined_Key),
               names_to = "date",
               values_to = "cases") %>%
  select(Admin2:cases) %>%
  mutate(date = mdy(date)) %>%
  select(-c(Lat, Long_))

US_deaths has one extra column, Population, which includes the population of each county. US_cases does not have this column. Because it sits right after Combined_Key, the pivot range for US_deaths ends at Population instead.

# from class lectures
US_deaths <- US_deaths %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -(UID:Population),
               names_to = "date",
               values_to = "deaths") %>%
  select(Admin2:deaths) %>%
  mutate(date = mdy(date)) %>%
  select(-c(Lat, Long_))

Now we have one row for each county and date.

Next, we’ll join US_cases and US_deaths into one US dataset:

# from class lectures
US <- US_cases %>%
  full_join(US_deaths)
## Joining with `by = join_by(Admin2, Province_State, Country_Region,
## Combined_Key, date)`

Next, we’ll check the dates the data covers.

# new analysis
range(US$date)
## [1] "2020-01-22" "2023-03-09"

The data runs from January 22, 2020 through March 9, 2023.

Visualizations

First, we’ll group the counties by state to get state totals. Next, we’ll add the states up for a national total. Finally, we’ll calculate deaths per million for each.

# from class lectures
US_by_state <- US %>%
  group_by(Province_State, Country_Region, date) %>%
  summarize(cases = sum(cases), deaths = sum(deaths),
            Population = sum(Population)) %>%
  mutate(deaths_per_mill = deaths * 1000000 / Population) %>%
  select(Province_State, Country_Region, date,
         cases, deaths, deaths_per_mill, Population) %>%
  ungroup()
## `summarise()` has regrouped the output.
## ℹ Summaries were computed grouped by Province_State, Country_Region, and date.
## ℹ Output is grouped by Province_State and Country_Region.
## ℹ Use `summarise(.groups = "drop_last")` to silence this message.
## ℹ Use `summarise(.by = c(Province_State, Country_Region, date))` for
##   per-operation grouping (`?dplyr::dplyr_by`) instead.
US_totals <- US_by_state %>%
  group_by(Country_Region, date) %>%
  summarize(cases = sum(cases), deaths = sum(deaths),
            Population = sum(Population)) %>%
  mutate(deaths_per_mill = deaths * 1000000 / Population) %>%
  select(Country_Region, date,
         cases, deaths, deaths_per_mill, Population) %>%
  ungroup()
## `summarise()` has regrouped the output.
## ℹ Summaries were computed grouped by Country_Region and date.
## ℹ Output is grouped by Country_Region.
## ℹ Use `summarise(.groups = "drop_last")` to silence this message.
## ℹ Use `summarise(.by = c(Country_Region, date))` for per-operation grouping
##   (`?dplyr::dplyr_by`) instead.

Now we have two datasets: US_by_state, with one row for each state and date, and US_totals, with one row for each date for the whole US. We’ll use these for the charts and tables below.

We’ll set the start date, so every chart below uses the same date

# new analysis
chart_start <- as.Date("2020-03-01")

Note on the start date: The time charts below start in March 2020. I chose that date because that’s when COVID-19 tests started to become available. Before then, few tests in the United States were available, as was widely reported at the time, so earlier case counts may undercount cases. The data itself begins on January 22, 2020, and the earlier dates are still in the tidied data, but not plotted on the charts.

Cumulative Cases and Deaths in New York

# from class lectures with modifications
# modification: chart starts in March 2020, the title shows the date range, the legend title is removed, and warning=FALSE is added to hide the log-scale warning
state <- "New York"
US_by_state %>%
  filter(Province_State == state) %>%
  filter(cases > 0) %>%
  filter(date >= chart_start) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = cases)) +
  geom_line(aes(color = "cases")) +
  geom_point(aes(color = "cases")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = deaths, color = "deaths")) +
  geom_point(aes(y = deaths, color = "deaths")) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90)) +
  labs(title = str_c("COVID19 in ", state, " (March 2020 to March 2023)"),
       y = NULL, color = NULL)

This chart plots New York’s cumulative cases and deaths on a log scale.

Next, we’ll check the final totals for cases and deaths for the US and for New York:

# new analysis
US_totals %>% slice_max(date) %>% select(date, cases, deaths)
## # A tibble: 1 × 3
##   date           cases  deaths
##   <date>         <dbl>   <dbl>
## 1 2023-03-09 103802702 1123836
US_by_state %>% filter(Province_State == state) %>% slice_max(date) %>% select(date, cases, deaths)
## # A tibble: 1 × 3
##   date         cases deaths
##   <date>       <dbl>  <dbl>
## 1 2023-03-09 6794738  77157

By March 9, 2023, New York had 6,794,738 cases and 77,157 deaths, and the US had 103,802,702 cases and 1,123,836 deaths.

Daily New Cases and Deaths

Next, we’ll calculate how many new cases and deaths there are each day with lag().

# from class lectures
max(US_totals$date)
## [1] "2023-03-09"
max(US_totals$deaths)
## [1] 1123836
US_by_state <- US_by_state %>%
  mutate(new_cases = cases - lag(cases),
         new_deaths = deaths - lag(deaths))

US_totals <- US_totals %>%
  mutate(new_cases = cases - lag(cases),
         new_deaths = deaths - lag(deaths))

tail(US_totals)
## # A tibble: 6 × 8
##   Country_Region date          cases deaths deaths_per_mill Population new_cases
##   <chr>          <date>        <dbl>  <dbl>           <dbl>      <dbl>     <dbl>
## 1 US             2023-03-04   1.04e8 1.12e6           3371.  332875137      2147
## 2 US             2023-03-05   1.04e8 1.12e6           3371.  332875137     -3862
## 3 US             2023-03-06   1.04e8 1.12e6           3371.  332875137      8564
## 4 US             2023-03-07   1.04e8 1.12e6           3372.  332875137     35371
## 5 US             2023-03-08   1.04e8 1.12e6           3374.  332875137     64861
## 6 US             2023-03-09   1.04e8 1.12e6           3376.  332875137     46931
## # ℹ 1 more variable: new_deaths <dbl>
tail(US_totals %>% select(new_cases, new_deaths, everything()))
## # A tibble: 6 × 8
##   new_cases new_deaths Country_Region date          cases deaths deaths_per_mill
##       <dbl>      <dbl> <chr>          <date>        <dbl>  <dbl>           <dbl>
## 1      2147          7 US             2023-03-04   1.04e8 1.12e6           3371.
## 2     -3862        -38 US             2023-03-05   1.04e8 1.12e6           3371.
## 3      8564         47 US             2023-03-06   1.04e8 1.12e6           3371.
## 4     35371        335 US             2023-03-07   1.04e8 1.12e6           3372.
## 5     64861        730 US             2023-03-08   1.04e8 1.12e6           3374.
## 6     46931        590 US             2023-03-09   1.04e8 1.12e6           3376.
## # ℹ 1 more variable: Population <dbl>

lag() subtracts the previous day’s total from each day’s total, which gives new cases and new deaths per day for the states and the US, such as 64,861 new cases and 730 new deaths on March 8, 2023.

We’ll plot daily new cases and deaths for the United States:

# from class lectures with modifications
# modification: chart starts in March 2020, the legend title is removed, and warning=FALSE is added to hide the log-scale warnings
US_totals %>%
  filter(date >= chart_start) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = new_cases)) +
  geom_line(aes(color = "new_cases")) +
  geom_point(aes(color = "new_cases")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = new_deaths, color = "new_deaths")) +
  geom_point(aes(y = new_deaths, color = "new_deaths")) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90)) +
  labs(title = "COVID19 in US", y = NULL, color = NULL)

This chart shows daily new cases and daily new deaths for the US, with one point for each day. The y-axis uses a log scale so cases and deaths can fit on the same axis.

Weekly New Cases and Deaths

Now we’ll add up daily counts by week.

# new analysis
US_weekly <- US_totals %>%
  mutate(week = floor_date(date, "week")) %>%
  group_by(week) %>%
  summarize(weekly_cases = sum(new_cases),
            weekly_deaths = sum(new_deaths),
            days = n()) %>%
  filter(days == 7)

Each bar on the next two charts represents one week.

# new analysis
US_weekly %>%
  filter(week >= chart_start) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = weekly_cases)) +
  geom_col(fill = "navy") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Weekly New COVID-19 Cases in the US",
       x = "Week", y = "New Cases per Week")

# new analysis
US_weekly %>%
  filter(week >= chart_start) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = weekly_deaths)) +
  geom_col(fill = "slateblue") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Weekly New COVID-19 Deaths in the US",
       x = "Week", y = "New Deaths per Week")

We’ll find the week with the most new cases and the week with the most new deaths:

# new analysis
US_weekly %>% slice_max(weekly_cases, n = 1) %>% select(week, weekly_cases)
## # A tibble: 1 × 2
##   week       weekly_cases
##   <date>            <dbl>
## 1 2022-01-09      5648759
US_weekly %>% slice_max(weekly_deaths, n = 1) %>% select(week, weekly_deaths)
## # A tibble: 1 × 2
##   week       weekly_deaths
##   <date>             <dbl>
## 1 2021-01-10         23429

The week of January 9, 2022 had the most new cases at 5,648,759, which is higher than previous peaks. The week of January 10, 2021 had the most new deaths at 23,429, a full year earlier. This reveals that the highest case counts and the highest death counts did not happen at the same time.

Comparing States: Deaths per Thousand

To compare states instead of looking at trends over time, we’ll build one row per state with cases and deaths per thousand residents, then look at the 10 states with the highest and lowest deaths per thousand:

# from class lectures
US_state_totals <- US_by_state %>%
  group_by(Province_State) %>%
  summarize(deaths = max(deaths), cases = max(cases),
            population = max(Population),
            cases_per_thou = 1000 * cases / population,
            deaths_per_thou = 1000 * deaths / population) %>%
  filter(cases > 0, population > 0)

US_state_totals %>%
  slice_max(deaths_per_thou, n = 10) %>%
  select(deaths_per_thou, cases_per_thou, everything())
## # A tibble: 10 × 6
##    deaths_per_thou cases_per_thou Province_State deaths   cases population
##              <dbl>          <dbl> <chr>           <dbl>   <dbl>      <dbl>
##  1            4.55           336. Arizona         33102 2443514    7278717
##  2            4.54           326. Oklahoma        17972 1290929    3956971
##  3            4.49           333. Mississippi     13370  990756    2976149
##  4            4.44           359. West Virginia    7960  642760    1792147
##  5            4.32           320. New Mexico       9061  670929    2096829
##  6            4.31           334. Arkansas        13020 1006883    3017804
##  7            4.29           335. Alabama         21032 1644533    4903185
##  8            4.28           368. Tennessee       29263 2515130    6829174
##  9            4.23           307. Michigan        42205 3064125    9986857
## 10            4.06           385. Kentucky        18130 1718471    4467673
US_state_totals %>%
  slice_min(deaths_per_thou, n = 10) %>%
  select(deaths_per_thou, cases_per_thou, everything())
## # A tibble: 10 × 6
##    deaths_per_thou cases_per_thou Province_State        deaths  cases population
##              <dbl>          <dbl> <chr>                  <dbl>  <dbl>      <dbl>

##  2           0.744           248. Northern Mariana Isl…     41 1.37e4      55144

##  4           1.30            269. Hawaii                  1841 3.81e5    1415872
##  5           1.49            245. Vermont                  929 1.53e5     623989
##  6           1.55            293. Puerto Rico             5823 1.10e6    3754939

Arizona, Oklahoma and Mississippi has the highest death rate at about 4.5 deaths per thousand residents and American Samoa is lowest at about 0.6.

Modeling

Modeling Death Rates from Case Rates

For this model, I wanted to see if states with more cases per thousand residents also have more deaths per thousand.

# from class lectures
mod <- lm(deaths_per_thou ~ cases_per_thou, data = US_state_totals)
summary(mod)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = deaths_per_thou ~ cases_per_thou, data = US_state_totals)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -2.3352 -0.5978  0.1491  0.6535  1.2086 
## 
## Coefficients:
##                Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)    -0.36167    0.72480  -0.499     0.62    
## cases_per_thou  0.01133    0.00232   4.881 9.76e-06 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 0.8615 on 54 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.3061, Adjusted R-squared:  0.2933 
## F-statistic: 23.82 on 1 and 54 DF,  p-value: 9.763e-06

This model estimates that deaths_per_thou is about -0.362 + 0.0113 * cases_per_thou. Each additional case per thousand residents is associated with about 0.011 more deaths per thousand.

Before generating predictions, we’ll check the range of cases_per_thou in the data:

# from class lectures
US_state_totals %>% slice_min(cases_per_thou)
## # A tibble: 1 × 6
##   Province_State deaths cases population cases_per_thou deaths_per_thou
##   <chr>           <dbl> <dbl>      <dbl>          <dbl>           <dbl>
## 1 American Samoa     34  8320      55641           150.           0.611
US_state_totals %>% slice_max(cases_per_thou)
## # A tibble: 1 × 6
##   Province_State deaths  cases population cases_per_thou deaths_per_thou
##   <chr>           <dbl>  <dbl>      <dbl>          <dbl>           <dbl>
## 1 Rhode Island     3870 460697    1059361           435.            3.65

Cases per thousand run from about 150 for American Samoa to 435 for Rhode Island. Next, we’ll add the model’s predictions to the state data.

# from class lectures
US_tot_w_pred <- US_state_totals %>% mutate(pred = predict(mod))
US_tot_w_pred
## # A tibble: 56 × 7
##    Province_State  deaths  cases population cases_per_thou deaths_per_thou  pred
##    <chr>            <dbl>  <dbl>      <dbl>          <dbl>           <dbl> <dbl>
##  1 Alabama          21032 1.64e6    4903185           335.           4.29   3.44
##  2 Alaska            1486 3.08e5     740995           415.           2.01   4.34
##  3 American Samoa      34 8.32e3      55641           150.           0.611  1.33
##  4 Arizona          33102 2.44e6    7278717           336.           4.55   3.44
##  5 Arkansas         13020 1.01e6    3017804           334.           4.31   3.42
##  6 California      101159 1.21e7   39512223           307.           2.56   3.12
##  7 Colorado         14181 1.76e6    5758736           306.           2.46   3.11
##  8 Connecticut      12220 9.77e5    3565287           274.           3.43   2.74
##  9 Delaware          3324 3.31e5     973764           340.           3.41   3.49
## 10 District of Co…   1432 1.78e5     705749           252.           2.03   2.49
## # ℹ 46 more rows

We’ll plot the actual values against the model’s predictions.

# from class lectures
US_tot_w_pred %>% ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x = cases_per_thou, y = deaths_per_thou), color = "blue") +
  geom_point(aes(x = cases_per_thou, y = pred), color = "red")

The model tells us that states with more cases per thousand tend to have more deaths per thousand. But the states are scattered widely around the line at every case rate. For example, Utah has about 1.7 deaths per thousand while Arizona has about 4.5.

Some of the questions this model raises, but cannot answer include: * What is different about states with similar case rates but very different death rates? * Would variables like population density, lockdown measures, or political affiliation help explain that gap?

Conclusion

Bias Statement

I worked on COVID data in an extremely nuanced way and lost family members to COVID in early 2020. As a result, I found it difficult to work on this assignment. To mitigate this, I kept the prose as plain as possible, thinking of it more like a set of instructions.

Conclusion

This report covers analysis done in class and new analysis that examines the Johns Hopkins (JHU) Center for Systems Science and Engineering (CSSE) Data. From this analysis, we can come to a few conclusions about the data. We can see that cases and deaths came in waves. The 7-day-period with the most new cases was the week of January 9, 2022, with about 5.6 million, and the 7-day-period with the most new deaths was the week of January 10, 2021, with about 23,400. By March 9, 2023, the US had recorded 103,802,702 cases and 1,123,836 deaths. Our analysis also shows us that states had very different death rates per thousand residents, but without additional data beyond this dataset, we can’t evaluate why this is the case.

From the data, we can tell that Arizona, Oklahoma and Mississippi had the highest death rates and American Samoa, the Northern Mariana Islands and Hawaii had the lowest. We also learned that higher case rates usually mean higher death rates, but that differs widely from state to state. Utah and Arizona had about the same case rate, at around 335-340 per 1,000 people, but Arizona had about 4.5 deaths per 1,000 compared to Utah with 1.7 deaths per 1,000.
